acetaminophen-toxicity.name: Acetaminophen toxicity
acetaminophen-toxicity.scope: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, 4-hour post-ingestion level, toxic metabolite NAPQI, N-acetylcysteine indications and timing, acute liver failure
acetaminophen-toxicity.core: Potentially toxic acetaminophen ingestion can be asymptomatic initially; time-specific concentration and hepatic injury determine immediate N-acetylcysteine treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Intentional overdose, repeated excessive dosing, unrecognized combination cold/pain products

rows.label: Clues

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CYP metabolism produces NAPQI; glutathione depletion → centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Known acute ingestion → **acetaminophen concentration at ≥4 hours**; earlier result cannot risk-stratify
★ Plot **Rumack–Matthew nomogram**, 4–24 h; treatment line starts 150 µg/mL at 4 h
Unknown timing/repeated supratherapeutic use → no nomogram; obtain concentration, AST/ALT, INR, glucose, creatinine
Delayed absorption and initial detectable subthreshold level → repeat concentration after 4–6 h
Assess co-ingestions/pregnancy; intentional ingestion → psychiatric safety evaluation after stabilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ At/above treatment line → **N-acetylcysteine**, ideally within 8 h; benefit persists when delayed
Likely substantial ingestion and result delayed beyond 8 h → start antidote while awaiting testing
Unknown time: >10 µg/mL or liver injury; repeated excess: ≥20 µg/mL or abnormal aminotransferases → treat
Recent acute overdose, protected airway → activated charcoal, usually within 4 h; toxicology consultation
Continue antidote until clearance and hepatic/coagulation recovery criteria met; acute liver failure → transplant center

rows.label: Complications
items: Fulminant hepatic failure, AKI, cerebral edema, hypoglycemia, death
IV antidote → non-IgE-mediated infusion reaction; pause/treat reaction, then resume when needed

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Count acetaminophen across all products**, avoid duplicate dosing, secure storage
Assess suicide risk and arrange mental-health care after deliberate ingestion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ischemic hepatitis: preceding profound hypotension
Viral hepatitis: exposure/serology without toxic ingestion pattern

rows.label: Prevention

items: Osteosarcoma: adolescence, hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1), prior radiation, Paget disease; chondrosarcoma: older adults
Hereditary multiple exostoses predispose to osteochondromas; most adult malignant bone lesions are metastases

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Night/rest pain**, enlarging mass, constitutional symptoms or pathologic fracture → concerning lesion
Osteoid osteoma: nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs; small cortical nidus
Osteochondroma: painless metaphyseal exostosis with medullary continuity; new growth after maturity concerning
Known cancer + constant back pain, vertebral point tenderness → **spinal metastasis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor lineage determines osteoid, cartilage or primitive-cell production; aggressive growth destroys cortex
Giant cell tumor: neoplastic stromal cells recruit osteoclast-like giant cells, causing locally aggressive osteolysis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Plain radiographs first**; assess location, margins, periosteal reaction and matrix
Aggressive lesion → MRI entire involved bone/adjacent joint; chest CT for lung metastases
★ **Orthopedic oncology plans biopsy tract**; core biopsy after imaging, before definitive treatment
CBC, ESR/CRP if infection suspected; normal labs do not exclude malignancy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Osteosarcoma → **neoadjuvant chemotherapy + wide resection**, then postoperative chemotherapy
Ewing → systemic chemotherapy plus surgery and/or radiation
Chondrosarcoma → wide surgical excision; conventional tumors relatively chemo/radioresistant
Symptomatic osteoid osteoma → radiofrequency ablation; asymptomatic osteochondroma → observation
Giant cell tumor → curettage/reconstruction; selected unresectable lesions → denosumab

rows.label: Complications
items: Pathologic fracture, neurovascular compromise, pulmonary metastases; limb surgery and chemotherapy morbidity
Mandible metastasis → mental nerve anesthesia (**numb chin**)

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: infection markers, cultures; may closely resemble Ewing
Bone metastases: older adult, multiple lesions; myeloma: anemia, monoclonal protein
Unicameral bone cyst: child, lucent expansile proximal humerus lesion; pathologic fracture after minor trauma

bone-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

brain-abscess.name: Brain abscess
brain-abscess.scope: Direct spread (otitis media, mastoiditis, sinusitis), hematogenous spread (endocarditis, cyanotic congenital heart disease), ring-enhancing lesion, polymicrobial, aspiration, empiric antibiotics
brain-abscess.core: Headache with a focal deficit or seizure and an enhancing intracranial mass after infection should prompt urgent abscess evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Otitis/mastoiditis → temporal lobe or cerebellum; sinusitis/dental infection → frontal lobe
Endocarditis, cyanotic congenital heart disease, pulmonary infection → hematogenous seeding, often multiple lesions
Neurosurgery/penetrating trauma → staphylococci; immunosuppression → fungi, Nocardia, Toxoplasma

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever may be absent; nausea, papilledema or deteriorating consciousness suggest increased ICP
★ **Ring enhancement with central diffusion restriction** strongly favors pyogenic abscess

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Focal cerebritis progresses to encapsulated pus with surrounding vasogenic edema
Contiguous infections often polymicrobial: streptococci and anaerobes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI with DWI** preferred; contrast CT if MRI unavailable
Blood cultures before antibiotics; aspirated material → aerobic/anaerobic cultures and targeted molecular testing
★ **Avoid LP**: low diagnostic yield, mass-effect herniation risk
Search source: ENT/dental assessment; echocardiography for bacteremia, multiple lesions, or endocarditis signs

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Ceftriaxone + metronidazole**; add vancomycin for trauma, neurosurgery, or staphylococcal concern
Urgent neurosurgical aspiration/drainage for sizable accessible lesions, mass effect, or diagnostic uncertainty
Small stable lesions may receive antibiotics with serial MRI; usual IV course 6–8 weeks
Stable, aspiration within 24 hours → cultures first may be reasonable; never delay antibiotics if deteriorating
Dexamethasone only for severe edema/impending herniation; levetiracetam for seizures

rows.label: Complications
items: Intraventricular rupture, ventriculitis, herniation, persistent focal deficits, epilepsy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat contiguous infection and endocarditis; correct infectious source and relevant cardiac lesions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Necrotic tumor: central diffusion restriction less typical, no infectious source
Toxoplasmosis: advanced HIV, multiple basal ganglia lesions
Neurocysticercosis: cyst with scolex, exposure in endemic region

brain-death.name: Brain death
brain-death.scope: Prerequisites (normothermia, normal BP), clinical exam (coma, absent brainstem reflexes), apnea test, ancillary testing (cerebral blood flow studies)
brain-death.core: Permanent loss of all brain function, including brainstem function, constitutes death; a beating heart on ventilation does not negate the diagnosis.

rows.label: Principle
items: Known catastrophic irreversible brain injury; compatible neuroimaging; adequate observation period
No family consent needed; after declaration → stop ventilator, unless organ donation planned

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Prerequisites: **temperature ≥36°C**, adult SBP ≥100 and MAP ≥75 mm Hg
Exclude paralysis/metabolic confounders; sedatives: ≥5 half-lives, longer if impaired clearance
★ Examination: **coma**, no brain-mediated motor response; absent brainstem reflexes (table)

rows.label: Don't
items: Oculocephalic testing with possible cervical injury; use caloric testing after confirming ear integrity
Declare death with any brain-mediated response or spontaneous breath
Use ancillary testing to bypass hypothermia or high CNS-depressant levels

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Spinal reflex movements may persist without contradicting diagnosis
Incomplete examination or unsafe apnea test → radionuclide cerebral perfusion or catheter angiography
After temperature ≤35.5°C, wait ≥24 hours following rewarming to ≥36°C

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Apnea test: no breaths, **PaCO2 ≥60 and ≥20 above baseline**, pH <7.30
Preoxygenate; abort apnea testing for hypotension, hypoxemia or unstable arrhythmia
★ 2023 update: **EEG no longer accepted** as ancillary testing; pediatric requirements differ

brain-tumors.name: Brain tumors
brain-tumors.scope: Metastatic brain tumors, glioblastoma, meningioma, pediatric tumors (medulloblastoma), vestibular schwannoma
brain-tumors.core: Progressive focal deficits, new seizures or headache with raised intracranial pressure require brain imaging for a mass lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known lung, breast, melanoma, renal or colorectal malignancy → brain metastases
Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema; altered consciousness or pupillary asymmetry → impending herniation
Frontal → personality change; posterior fossa → ataxia; temporal (Meyer loop) → contralateral **superior quadrantanopia**
Pediatric posterior fossa mass can obstruct CSF flow and rapidly cause hydrocephalus
★ **Anosmia**, normal nasal exam, frontal release signs, papilledema → **subfrontal olfactory groove meningioma**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema
Fixed cranial volume makes expanding tissue/CSF raise pressure and threaten brainstem perfusion
Astrocytoma grade, prognosis → **degree of histologic anaplasia**, not metastasis; extracranial spread rare

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI brain** best defines mass, edema and multiplicity; CT for unstable patients
Metastatic pattern → search primary with chest/abdominal imaging; tissue diagnosis when needed
★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Tinnitus, imbalance, facial weakness/numbness, altered taste (CN VII, V) → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic edema → **dexamethasone**; herniation → head elevation, hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency neurosurgery
Seizure → levetiracetam; no routine antiseizure prophylaxis for every seizure-naive tumor patient
★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children
Craniopharyngioma resection disrupts pituitary stalk → **lifelong pituitary hormone replacement**; watch central DI

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive hydrocephalus, herniation, hemorrhage, persistent neurologic deficits
Radiation injury, cognitive decline, steroid hyperglycemia and infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Abscess: infection context and central diffusion restriction
Primary CNS lymphoma: often periventricular; steroids can obscure biopsy
Stroke: abrupt maximal onset with vascular distribution; chronic subdural: prior head trauma
Ménière disease: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss

table.title: Tumor distinctions
rows: Months of headache, deficits; necrotic, crosses corpus callosum
Woman; extra-axial, uniform enhancement, dural tail; parasagittal
Child; midline cerebellar mass; CSF drop metastases
CPA; insidious, high-frequency unilateral sensorineural hearing loss
Child; ataxia, nystagmus, head tilt, cranial neuropathies

carbon-monoxide-poisoning.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.scope: Carboxyhemoglobin, pulse oximetry pitfall, normobaric and hyperbaric oxygen indications, delayed neurologic sequelae
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.core: Headache, dizziness, nausea, or confusion affecting several people in an enclosed combustion setting suggests carbon monoxide exposure.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: House fires, faulty heaters, generators indoors, vehicle exhaust, poorly ventilated fuel-burning equipment
Pregnancy, infancy, anemia, and cardiopulmonary disease increase vulnerability at a given exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: Odorless gas: flulike illness without fever; symptoms improve outside exposure site
★ **Syncope, altered consciousness, focal deficits, chest pain**, or severe acidosis → serious toxicity
**Cherry-red/flushed skin, pink mucosa** + indoor coma → suspect CO; often absent, normal color not reassuring

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CO binds hemoglobin avidly, reduces oxygen carriage, shifts dissociation curve left
Mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation add tissue injury; fetal hemoglobin retains CO longer

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous or arterial co-oximetry** measures carboxyhemoglobin; draw promptly without delaying oxygen
★ **Normal pulse oximetry and PaO₂ do not exclude poisoning**; both can appear reassuring
COHb >2% in nonsmokers or >9% in smokers supports exposure; level poorly predicts outcome
ECG, troponin for cardiac injury; lactate/ABG for acidosis; pregnancy testing when relevant
Prior oxygen or delayed presentation lowers COHb; exposure history remains decisive

rows.label: Tx
items: Remove from source, protect rescuers, assess airway and ventilation
★ **100% oxygen by nonrebreather** immediately; intubate for coma or respiratory failure
Consider hyperbaric oxygen for neurologic impairment, loss of consciousness, cardiac injury, severe acidosis, or COHb >25–30%
Pregnancy → urgent hyperbaric consultation at lower severity/levels; treatment decisions integrate symptoms, not COHb alone
Smoke inhalation + profound lactic acidosis/shock → consider cyanide, give hydroxocobalamin

rows.label: Complications
items: Myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, death; delayed cognitive, behavioral, gait, or movement deficits after recovery
Follow-up for delayed neurologic symptoms; mild initial presentation does not exclude later deficits

rows.label: Prevention
items: Working CO detectors, professional heater inspection, never run generators or engines indoors
Public safety evaluation before returning to the exposure site

rows.label: Mimics
items: Viral illness: fever and infectious contacts rather than shared building exposure
Methemoglobinemia: cyanosis, saturation near 85%, chocolate-colored blood
Cyanide poisoning: rapid collapse, marked lactate elevation after enclosed fire

carotid-artery-stenosis.name: Carotid artery stenosis
carotid-artery-stenosis.scope: Asymptomatic carotid bruit, carotid duplex ultrasound, medical management, indications for carotid endarterectomy
carotid-artery-stenosis.core: Carotid atherosclerosis causes ipsilateral retinal or cerebral ischemia; intervention depends on symptoms, stenosis severity, and operative risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia; coronary or peripheral arterial disease
Prior neck radiation increases stenosis and surgical complexity

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Amaurosis fugax** (painless curtain-like monocular vision loss), contralateral weakness, aphasia → symptomatic disease
Bruit may be incidental; loudness does not measure severity, complete occlusion may be silent
Isolated dizziness or syncope rarely represents carotid-territory ischemia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plaque rupture → artery-to-artery emboli; critical narrowing can reduce cerebral perfusion
Retinal **Hollenhorst plaque** (cholesterol embolus) → ulcerated ipsilateral carotid plaque

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected stenosis or selected incidental bruit evaluation → **carotid duplex ultrasound**
CTA/MRA confirms anatomy before intervention; brain imaging evaluates neurologic deficits
★ **No routine screening** of asymptomatic general adults; bruit auscultation is an unreliable screen

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All: **antiplatelet + high-intensity statin**, BP and diabetes control
Symptomatic operative candidates: endarterectomy generally within **2 weeks**, after neurologic stabilization
Classic asymptomatic CEA criteria: ≥70%, life expectancy ≥3–5 years, perioperative stroke/death <3%; individualized decision
CREST-2: asymptomatic stenting benefited selected patients; CEA lacked significant benefit; avoid automatic surgery
Symptomatic older adults: CEA generally preferred to stenting; high surgical-risk anatomy may favor stenting

rows.label: Complications
items: Ischemic stroke, recurrent TIAs; procedure → stroke, MI, cranial nerve injury
Hyperperfusion after revascularization → headache, seizures, brain hemorrhage; driven by **postoperative hypertension**
New deficit after endarterectomy → **noncontrast head CT** first: hemorrhage vs carotid thrombosis; no heparin/tPA beforehand
★ Expanding neck hematoma with stridor → **open wound/emergent neck exploration**; no imaging delay

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, Mediterranean-style diet; sustained vascular risk reduction
New focal neurologic symptoms → emergency stroke assessment, even after symptom resolution

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic stenosis: cardiac murmur radiates to both carotids
Cardioembolism: atrial fibrillation or cardiac thrombus; multiple vascular territories
Migraine aura: gradually spreading positive visual/sensory symptoms
Giant cell arteritis: headache, jaw claudication, ↑ESR; vision loss often persistent

table.title: Symptomatic ipsilateral stenosis
rows: Selected patients: age, sex, comorbidity matter

carpal-tunnel-syndrome.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
carpal-tunnel-syndrome.scope: Median nerve entrapment, pregnancy and endocrine risk factors, Phalen and Tinel tests, wrist splinting, corticosteroid injection, surgical release
carpal-tunnel-syndrome.core: Median nerve compression at the wrist causes nocturnal paresthesias in the thumb, index, middle, and radial ring fingers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pregnancy/fluid retention, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis
Forceful repetitive hand activity, wrist trauma; dialysis-associated amyloid in selected patients

rows.label: Clues
items: Shaking hand relieves symptoms; driving or sustained wrist flexion aggravates symptoms
★ **Thenar weakness/atrophy**, dropping objects, impaired thumb opposition → advanced nerve injury
Central palm sensation usually spared because palmar cutaneous branch bypasses tunnel
Bilateral symptoms common; isolated little-finger symptoms argue against median neuropathy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Raised pressure beneath transverse carpal ligament → median nerve ischemia/demyelination
Long-standing compression progresses to axonal loss and persistent motor impairment

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical history + **Phalen/Tinel or carpal compression** findings support clinical diagnosis
Phalen: sustained wrist flexion; Tinel: percussion over median nerve reproduces distal paresthesia
★ **Nerve-conduction studies/EMG** for atypical presentation, severity assessment, or uncertain diagnosis before surgery
Targeted TSH/glucose testing when systemic disease suspected; routine wrist imaging unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Mild/moderate or **pregnancy** → **neutral-position night wrist splint**, ergonomics; pregnancy often resolves postpartum
Local corticosteroid injection for persistent symptoms or short-term relief
★ Severe deficit, denervation, or failed conservative care → **surgical carpal tunnel release**
NSAIDs do not relieve the underlying compression; avoid repeated ineffective analgesic-only management

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent sensory loss and thenar wasting if severe compression persists
Injection → transient hyperglycemia, rare nerve injury; surgery → scar pain or incomplete release

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reduce prolonged wrist flexion/extension and forceful vibration; adjust workstation and tools
Manage contributing endocrine/inflammatory disease; reassess worsening motor function promptly

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cervical radiculopathy: neck pain, dermatomal weakness/reflex changes
Ulnar neuropathy: little finger/ulnar ring symptoms, interosseous weakness
Pronator syndrome: proximal forearm pain with palmar sensory involvement

carpal-tunnel-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established peripheral nerve localization and management.

cerebral-palsy.name: Cerebral palsy
cerebral-palsy.scope: Spastic diplegia, spastic hemiplegia, spastic quadriplegia, dyskinetic (athetoid) cerebral palsy, ataxic, prematurity and intraventricular hemorrhage risk, hyperreflexia, contractures, multidisciplinary management
cerebral-palsy.core: Persistent abnormal posture and movement from a nonprogressive injury to the developing brain; functional manifestations change with growth.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prematurity, periventricular leukomalacia, intraventricular hemorrhage, perinatal stroke
Congenital infection, brain malformation, neonatal hypoxic-ischemic injury, kernicterus

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Delayed motor milestones**, persistent primitive reflexes, abnormal tone; early hand preference suggests hemiplegia
Spasticity: velocity-dependent tone, hyperreflexia, clonus, extensor plantar responses
Feeding difficulty, drooling, asymmetric posture; cognition may be normal

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immature motor pathways injured before, during, or shortly after birth; injury itself remains static

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical developmental/neurologic assessment**; brain MRI defines injury pattern or malformation
Assess hearing, vision, communication, nutrition, epilepsy, and intellectual function
Loss of acquired skills or progressive weakness → metabolic/genetic evaluation rather than presumed cerebral palsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Early multidisciplinary rehabilitation**: physical, occupational, speech and feeding support
Focal spasticity → botulinum toxin; generalized troublesome spasticity → oral baclofen
Severe refractory spasticity → intrathecal baclofen or selected dorsal rhizotomy
Orthoses, mobility aids; fixed contractures/hip displacement → orthopedic evaluation
Treat seizures; swallowing assessment and enteral feeding when aspiration or inadequate intake

rows.label: Complications
items: Contractures, hip subluxation, scoliosis, pain, osteoporosis; aspiration, malnutrition, epilepsy
Musculoskeletal deformities can progress despite static brain lesion

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Antenatal magnesium sulfate** for imminent early preterm birth reduces cerebral palsy risk
Treat severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia; therapeutic hypothermia for eligible neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Hip surveillance, stretching, adequate nutrition reduce secondary disability

rows.label: Mimics
items: Muscular dystrophy: progressive proximal weakness, elevated CK
Dopa-responsive dystonia: diurnal fluctuation, marked levodopa response

cerebral-palsy.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric neurology and perinatal prevention teaching.

cervical-radiculopathy.name: Cervical radiculopathy
cervical-radiculopathy.scope: C5-C8 radiculopathy, cervical disc herniation, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, LMN arm and UMN leg signs, Spurling test, conservative management, MRI cervical spine, surgical decompression
cervical-radiculopathy.core: Neck pain radiating down one arm with a dermatomal sensory deficit and reduced corresponding reflex.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Disc herniation in younger adults; osteophytes and foraminal narrowing with aging
Repetitive neck loading, smoking, prior cervical injury

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Spurling test**: extension, ipsilateral rotation, axial compression reproduce arm symptoms
Shoulder abduction may relieve root pain
★ **Myelopathy**: hand clumsiness, gait imbalance, LMN arms plus UMN legs; late bladder dysfunction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Root compression → segmental weakness; central canal stenosis → spinal cord dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: Map strength, sensation, reflexes; examine gait, plantar responses, Hoffmann sign
★ **Cervical MRI**: myelopathy, progressive deficit, cancer/infection concern, or failed conservative care
EMG/nerve conduction studies if localization uncertain; sensory responses usually preserved in radiculopathy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated: **NSAIDs + physical therapy**, activity modification; most improve within weeks
Persistent disabling root pain → consider epidural steroid injection or surgical referral
Cord compression or progressive motor deficit → urgent spine evaluation for decompression
Avoid cervical manipulation with suspected myelopathy

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent denervation and muscle atrophy; untreated cord compression → irreversible disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: Ergonomic adjustments, neck strengthening, smoking cessation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Carpal tunnel: median hand symptoms, positive Phalen, no neck provocation
Rotator cuff disease: painful shoulder motion, preserved distal neurologic examination
Brachial plexopathy: multiple roots/nerves, abnormal sensory nerve responses
ALS: mixed UMN/LMN signs, no sensory loss

cervical-spine-injury.name: Cervical spine injury
cervical-spine-injury.scope: Whiplash, cervical strain, NEXUS criteria, Canadian C-spine rule, cervical fractures (odontoid, hangman, burst), atlantoaxial subluxation, spinal clearance
cervical-spine-injury.core: After trauma, protect the neck until a reliable low-risk examination or imaging excludes clinically significant cervical injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High-energy collision, axial load, falls in older adults; osteoporosis
Rheumatoid arthritis, Down syndrome → atlantoaxial instability

rows.label: Clues
items: Midline tenderness, paresthesias, weakness; high cord injury may impair ventilation
Whiplash: **hyperextension** from rear impact; muscle spasm, straightened lordosis, usually no neurologic deficit

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fracture or ligament disruption → instability; secondary motion may injure spinal cord

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **NEXUS**: alert; no intoxication, midline tenderness, focal deficit or distracting injury → clinical clearance
★ Canadian rule: **age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, or extremity paresthesias** → imaging
Low-risk features: simple rear-end collision, ambulatory, seated, delayed neck pain, or no midline tenderness
Low-risk feature present + active rotation 45° each way → clear; otherwise image
★ Imaging → **CT cervical spine**; deficit/ligament concern → MRI; older exam questions may expect lateral x-ray

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway with manual inline stabilization; immobilize suspected unstable injury and obtain spine consultation
Unstable fracture or cord compression → stabilization/decompression; avoid routine high-dose methylprednisolone
Uncomplicated strain after clearance: NSAIDs, early gentle mobilization and exercise; avoid prolonged soft-collar use
Negative high-quality CT usually permits collar removal without neurologic concern; discordant findings → spine consultation

rows.label: Complications
items: Spinal cord injury, respiratory failure, neurogenic shock; immobilization → pressure injury and stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seat belts, helmets, fall prevention; avoid axial loading during diving
★ **Do not force neck movement** in an unreliable examination or high-risk patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Muscular strain: paraspinal pain after dangerous injury excluded
Degenerative stenosis: chronic symptoms; may predispose to cord injury after minor trauma

table.title: Important patterns
rows: C2 dens; type II nonunion risk
Axial compression; retropulsion may injure cord
Axial load; transverse ligament injury may destabilize

cranial-nerve-palsies.name: Cranial nerve palsies
cranial-nerve-palsies.scope: CN III palsy, CN IV palsy, CN VI palsy, Bell palsy (CN VII, hyperacusis, corticosteroids), microvascular diabetic neuropathy, cavernous sinus thrombosis
cranial-nerve-palsies.core: Localize diplopia by the weak extraocular muscle; distinguish peripheral facial paralysis from a central lesion by forehead involvement.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, hypertension → ischemic mononeuropathy; trauma → trochlear injury
Sinusitis or facial infection → cavernous sinus thrombosis; pregnancy associated with Bell palsy

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **CN III/IV/VI palsy + V1/V2 numbness, proptosis** → cavernous sinus lesion; fever, chemosis → thrombosis
Bell palsy: unilateral upper/lower facial weakness, altered taste, hyperacusis; no other focal deficits
Raised ICP may produce unilateral or bilateral abducens palsy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Diabetic ischemia often spares superficial parasympathetic CN III fibers; compression threatens pupil function
CN VII inflammation within facial canal disrupts facial movement and stapedius innervation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute CN III palsy → urgent **CTA/MRA**, especially painful or pupil-involving; exclude aneurysm
Typical isolated Bell palsy: clinical; atypical/recurrent palsy → MRI, targeted Lyme testing
Suspected cavernous thrombosis → contrast MRI/MRV or CT venography; blood cultures
Isolated diabetic microvascular CN VI palsy: **brain MRI usually normal**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Bell palsy within 72 hours → **prednisone**; add valacyclovir for severe paralysis
★ Artificial tears, nighttime ointment and eyelid taping to protect exposed cornea
Cavernous thrombosis: IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole; source drainage, consider anticoagulation
Microvascular palsy: vascular risk control, temporary patch/prism; reassess if persistent or progressive

rows.label: Complications
items: Exposure keratitis, corneal ulceration; facial synkinesis after recovery
Septic thrombosis → meningitis, stroke, blindness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat facial/sinus infections; optimize diabetes and BP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Stroke: forehead relatively spared with contralateral limb findings
Myasthenia: fatigable variable weakness, normal pupils
Ramsay Hunt: ear vesicles and otalgia with facial paralysis
Carotid-cavernous fistula: post-traumatic **pulsatile proptosis, orbital bruit**, chemosis

table.title: Ocular localization
rows: Worse downstairs; compensatory opposite head tilt

cranial-nerve-palsies.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-ophthalmology and Bell palsy teaching.

dementia.name: Dementia
dementia.scope: Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, reversible causes, normal cognitive aging vs MCI, Parkinson disease dementia
dementia.core: Acquired cognitive decline interfering with independent daily function; distinguish dementia from normal aging and mild cognitive impairment by functional consequences.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced age: strongest Alzheimer risk; early-onset first-degree family history; Down syndrome (APP triplication)
Vascular risk factors, prior stroke, Parkinson disease
Anticholinergics, sedatives, alcohol, hearing loss, sleep apnea may worsen cognition

rows.label: Clues
items: Collateral history: missed bills/medications, getting lost, unsafe cooking or driving
Personality, language, executive, visuospatial, memory, motor symptoms help establish phenotype
Abrupt change, fluctuating attention, fever, focal deficits → evaluate acute superimposed illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alzheimer: amyloid plaques/tau tangles; Lewy/Parkinson: alpha-synuclein; vascular disease: ischemic neuronal injury
Alzheimer: hippocampal loss → poor delayed/episodic recall; **nucleus basalis of Meynert** loss → acetylcholine deficit
Frontotemporal degeneration affects frontal/anterior temporal networks, often before typical late-life onset

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Patient/informant history, cognition, function**; MoCA/MMSE support diagnosis, cannot establish it alone
★ **CBC, CMP, TSH, B12**, depression/medication review; HIV/syphilis testing if risk
Brain MRI or noncontrast CT → infarcts, mass, subdural, hydrocephalus; avoid routine PET as first test
Normal aging: slower retrieval, preserved independence → reassurance; MCI: objective deficit, independence preserved
Typical Alzheimer: clinical diagnosis after routine labs/imaging; **APOE genotyping not indicated**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Alzheimer/Lewy/Parkinson dementia → **donepezil or rivastigmine**; moderate/severe Alzheimer → add memantine
Vascular disease → BP/lipid/diabetes control, stroke prevention; frontotemporal behavioral symptoms → consider SSRI
★ Agitation → seek pain/infection, routines/redirection first; **avoid typical antipsychotics in Lewy/Parkinson disease**
Early biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer: specialist-selected antiamyloid drugs; baseline/serial MRI for ARIA
Parkinson dementia psychosis/agitation → **quetiapine** over haloperidol; clozapine needs agranulocytosis monitoring

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, malnutrition, wandering, caregiver burnout; antipsychotics → increased mortality
Cholinesterase inhibitors → bradycardia, syncope, GI effects; antiamyloid antibodies → edema/microhemorrhage
Parkinson disease: dementia strongest predictor of nursing home placement and mortality

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Driving/home safety, advance planning**, caregiver support; assess decision-specific capacity
Visuospatial deficit, e.g., failed pentagon copy → **no car keys** until formal driving assessment
Exercise, hearing correction, social engagement, vascular risk reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Delirium: hours–days, impaired attention, fluctuating awareness
Depression: prominent distress, variable effort, potentially reversible cognitive deficits
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus: gait-first decline, incontinence, ventriculomegaly; tap test may predict shunt response

table.title: Phenotype clues
rows: Insidious episodic-memory decline, later multidomain deficits
Stroke-related or stepwise decline, focal findings
Early hallucinations, fluctuation, REM behavior, parkinsonism
Early disinhibition/apathy or progressive aphasia; memory spared
Established motor disease >1 year before dementia

dementia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [Alzheimer's Association diagnostic guidance 2024](https://www.alz.org/news/2024/clinical-practice-guideline-evaluation-alzheimers), [NICE dementia](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations/); established subtype teaching.

encephalitis.name: Encephalitis
encephalitis.scope: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1), temporal lobe lesions, CSF analysis (elevated RBCs, lymphocytic pleocytosis, PCR), IV acyclovir, West Nile virus, autoimmune encephalitis
encephalitis.core: Fever with sustained altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits suggests brain inflammation and warrants immediate empiric acyclovir.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: HSV-1 often occurs without immunosuppression; mosquito exposure suggests arboviruses
Autoimmune disease or tumor association; anti-NMDA receptor disease sometimes accompanies ovarian teratoma
Neonate, days–weeks old: perinatal HSV → seizures, fever, CSF RBCs, negative Gram stain

rows.label: Clues
items: HSV: personality change, aphasia, olfactory hallucinations, focal seizures
★ **Temporal lobe abnormalities** strongly suggest HSV; hemorrhagic CSF possible but not required
West Nile: movement disorder or asymmetric flaccid weakness; anti-NMDA: psychosis, dyskinesia, autonomic instability
Paraneoplastic limbic: **small cell lung cancer**, subacute psychosis/memory loss, medial temporal lesions, negative HSV PCR

rows.label: Pathophys
items: HSV causes necrotizing inflammation, often limbic/temporal; mosquito-borne viruses infect neuronal tissue
Autoantibodies against neuronal surface antigens disrupt synaptic signaling

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **LP: CSF cells, protein, glucose, HSV PCR**; lymphocytes, ↑protein, usually normal glucose
Neuroimaging before LP for focal deficits, papilledema, marked impaired consciousness, or suspected mass effect
MRI more sensitive than CT; EEG identifies nonconvulsive seizures or temporal periodic discharges
Early negative PCR with strong suspicion → continue treatment and repeat CSF PCR in 3–7 days
West Nile: CSF IgM; autoimmune suspicion → CSF/serum antibodies and tumor search

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected HSV → **IV acyclovir immediately**, usually 14–21 days; do not await PCR
Airway/seizure support; possible bacterial infection → ceftriaxone + vancomycin; Listeria risk → add ampicillin
Acyclovir: renal adjustment, IV hydration; West Nile: supportive care
★ Autoimmune disease → **steroids, IVIG/plasma exchange**, tumor removal after infectious evaluation
Reduced consciousness, status epilepticus, or respiratory compromise → ICU-level care

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent memory impairment, epilepsy, focal deficits, death; acyclovir crystal nephropathy
Severe autoimmune disease: arrhythmia, hypoventilation, prolonged rehabilitation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Mosquito repellent, protective clothing, vector control; no routine HSV encephalitis vaccine

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bacterial meningitis: neutrophilic CSF, low glucose; overlap requires empiric coverage
Toxic/metabolic delirium: systemic explanation without inflammatory CSF
Primary psychosis: lacks new seizures, dysautonomia, or focal neurologic abnormalities
Rabies: animal/bat exposure, **hydrophobia**, hypersalivation, agitation

encephalitis.evidence: Not checked online; established infectious and autoimmune neurology teaching.

epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
epilepsy.scope: Focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, absence seizures, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, EEG findings, antiepileptic therapy (valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine), lifestyle counseling
epilepsy.core: Recurrent unprovoked seizures reflect epilepsy; classify focal versus generalized onset before choosing a maintenance antiseizure drug.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior brain injury, stroke, CNS infection, developmental lesions, genetic predisposition
Sleep deprivation, alcohol withdrawal and missed drugs can precipitate seizures; provoked seizures alone ≠ epilepsy

rows.label: Clues
items: Focal onset: aura, unilateral motor activity, automatisms or impaired awareness; may evolve bilaterally
Generalized tonic-clonic: abrupt loss of consciousness, stiffening/jerking, postictal confusion, lateral tongue injury
Absence: staring, immediate recovery; JME: morning myoclonus ± generalized convulsions
Infantile spasms: flexion clusters, **hypsarrhythmia** on EEG; standard antiseizure drugs ineffective

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormally synchronized cortical neuronal discharges impair awareness, sensation or motor function
Excitatory/inhibitory imbalance may arise from structural lesions or inherited channel/network dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **EEG and epilepsy-protocol MRI** after unprovoked seizure; normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy
Epilepsy: ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart, or one with high recurrence risk/defined syndrome
Check glucose/electrolytes and provoking causes; urgent CT for trauma, focal deficit or persistent altered consciousness
Absence: generalized **3-Hz spike-wave**, provoked by hyperventilation; JME: generalized polyspike-wave
Child, nocturnal facial twitching/drooling, speech arrest + **centrotemporal spikes** → benign rolandic epilepsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Convulsion **≥5 minutes** → airway/glucose, **lorazepam**, then IV levetiracetam/fosphenytoin/valproate
Focal epilepsy → lamotrigine or levetiracetam; generalized tonic-clonic/JME → broad-spectrum agent
★ Valproate effective for generalized syndromes; **avoid when pregnancy possible** if alternatives effective
Pure absence → ethosuximide; absence + tonic-clonic → broad-spectrum drug; infantile spasms → **ACTH or vigabatrin**
Avoid carbamazepine/phenytoin for absence/myoclonic syndromes; drug-resistant focal disease → surgical evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Status epilepticus, injury, aspiration, SUDEP; valproate → hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, teratogenicity
Lamotrigine → serious rash with rapid titration
Levetiracetam → irritability/mood symptoms; depression history + high recurrence risk → continue, monitor mood
Erythromycin (CYP3A4 inhibitor) ↑carbamazepine → ataxia, somnolence, diplopia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adherence, regular sleep, avoid alcohol excess; no abrupt drug withdrawal
Driving restrictions follow local law; no unsupervised swimming/heights; preconception folate and drug review
Pregnancy lowers antiseizure levels; breakthrough seizures → **increase current drug dose**, avoid switching

rows.label: Mimics
items: Syncope: prodrome, rapid recovery; brief jerks possible
Psychogenic nonepileptic events: video-EEG confirms typical event without epileptic correlate

table.title: Focal seizure localization
rows: Epigastric/olfactory aura, lip-smacking automatisms; superior quadrantanopia

epilepsy.evidence: Pregnancy recommendations checked 2026-10-30: [AAN/AES/SMFM 2024](https://www.aan.com/PressRoom/Home/PressRelease/5170); classification established teaching.

erectile-dysfunction.name: Erectile dysfunction
erectile-dysfunction.scope: Psychogenic vs organic (nocturnal penile tumescence), diabetes mellitus, vascular insufficiency, drug-induced, PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, nitrate contraindication), vacuum devices, penile prosthesis
erectile-dysfunction.core: Persistent difficulty obtaining or maintaining an erection warrants assessment of vascular health, medication effects, endocrine function, and psychological context.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, atherosclerosis, smoking, hypertension, pelvic surgery or radiation, spinal injury
SSRIs, thiazides, some beta-blockers, antipsychotics, heavy alcohol, daily cannabis; depression and performance anxiety

rows.label: Clues
items: Low libido and reduced spontaneous erections suggest androgen deficiency
Claudication or diminished peripheral pulses suggest vascular disease; penile curvature suggests Peyronie disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nitric oxide → cGMP → cavernosal smooth-muscle relaxation and arterial inflow; venous occlusion maintains rigidity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Sexual/medical history, medication review, genital/vascular examination; assess cardiovascular risk
★ **Morning total testosterone**, glucose/A1c, lipids; repeat low testosterone before diagnosing hypogonadism
Nocturnal tumescence testing or penile Doppler only if uncertainty or selected procedural planning

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Sildenafil or tadalafil** first-line oral options; sexual stimulation required
★ **Never combine PDE-5 inhibitors with nitrates or riociguat** → profound hypotension
**Stop culprits before PDE-5** (drugs, alcohol, cannabis); counseling, exercise; testosterone for confirmed hypogonadism
Oral failure → vacuum device or intracavernosal/intraurethral alprostadil; refractory cases → penile prosthesis
Unstable cardiac disease → stabilize before resuming sexual activity; alpha-blockers increase hypotension risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Relationship distress, depression; ED may precede symptomatic cardiovascular disease
Alprostadil: priapism; erection >4 hours → emergency evaluation; prosthesis infection or mechanical failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation; optimize glycemia, BP, lipids; reduce excess alcohol

rows.label: Mimics
items: Low libido alone: desire impaired without necessarily impaired erectile mechanics
Premature ejaculation: erection obtained but ejaculation earlier than desired

table.title: Etiologic clues
rows: Gradual, consistent, also with masturbation; nocturnal erections reduced
Heavy drinking, high GGT; nocturnal erections may persist

febrile-seizures.name: Febrile seizures
febrile-seizures.scope: Simple febrile seizures, complex febrile seizures, diagnostic evaluation, antipyretics and reassurance, recurrence risk
febrile-seizures.core: Seizure during fever in a child aged 6–60 months, without CNS infection, metabolic cause, or prior afebrile seizures.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young age, family history, viral febrile illness; often occurs early in illness
Recurrence more likely with first episode <18 months, lower fever, brief preceding fever, affected relative

rows.label: Clues
items: Transient postictal sleepiness followed by return to baseline; normal neurologic examination between events
★ **Meningismus, persistent altered mental status, toxic appearance**, or focal deficit → alternate urgent diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Age-dependent neuronal excitability lowers seizure threshold during inflammatory illness
Not caused by a particular temperature rise rate; fever can be recognized only after seizure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical simple event → **clinical diagnosis; evaluate fever source**, not routine EEG or brain imaging
Bedside glucose for ongoing seizure, prolonged altered state, or concerning metabolic context
★ Suspected meningitis → **LP**; consider at 6–12 months with incomplete Hib/pneumococcal immunization
Prior antibiotics may mask meningitis; complex features prompt individualized neurologic/CNS infection evaluation
No routine electrolyte panel after brief event with normal recovery and hydration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Ongoing seizure **>5 minutes → benzodiazepine**, airway positioning, oxygen, glucose assessment
Stopped seizure, well child → reassurance, hydration, identify and treat fever source
Acetaminophen or ibuprofen improves comfort; antipyretics do not reliably prevent future febrile seizures
No chronic phenobarbital or valproate for simple events; harms exceed preventive benefit

rows.label: Complications
items: Approximately one-third recur; simple episodes do not cause intellectual disability or brain damage
Later epilepsy risk low after simple events; higher with complex features or abnormal neurodevelopment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Parent plan: **side positioning, time event, nothing in mouth**; emergency help for prolonged seizure
Selected recurrent prolonged events → home rescue intranasal midazolam or rectal diazepam plan

rows.label: Mimics
items: Meningitis: sustained encephalopathy, meningeal signs, CSF inflammation
Rigors: preserved consciousness during shivering
Epilepsy: unprovoked events outside febrile illness

febrile-seizures.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric febrile seizure evaluation principles.

herpes-zoster.name: Herpes zoster
herpes-zoster.scope: Varicella zoster reactivation, dermatomal rash, herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, oral antivirals, postherpetic neuralgia, Shingrix vaccine
herpes-zoster.core: Latent varicella-zoster reactivation causes painful unilateral dermatomal vesicles; ophthalmic involvement or disseminated disease changes urgency and treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, HIV, malignancy, transplantation, immunosuppressive drugs
Previous chickenpox or live varicella vaccination establishes latency; no new exposure required

rows.label: Clues
items: Burning/allodynia can precede eruption by days; crops crust over approximately 7–10 days
★ **V1 distribution, nasal-tip lesions, eye pain** → urgent ophthalmology for zoster ophthalmicus
★ **Ear vesicles + ipsilateral facial paralysis** ± hearing/vestibular symptoms → Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Multiple noncontiguous dermatomes or >20 lesions outside primary/adjacent dermatomes suggests dissemination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced VZV-specific cellular immunity permits virus to travel from sensory ganglion to skin
Neuronal inflammation/injury explains acute pain and persistent neuropathic symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical eruption → **clinical diagnosis**; atypical lesions → vesicle-base VZV PCR
Assess ocular, neurologic, and systemic findings; consider immunodeficiency evaluation for unusually severe/recurrent disease
CSF PCR for suspected CNS infection; do not delay treatment in high-risk presentations

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Valacyclovir, famciclovir, or acyclovir** ideally within 72 hours; still treat new lesions or complications
Dissemination, visceral/CNS disease, severe immunosuppression → **IV acyclovir**
Acute pain: acetaminophen/NSAID, add neuropathic agent when needed; avoid routine systemic steroids
Ramsay Hunt: antiviral plus glucocorticoid early; eye lubrication/protection for incomplete closure
Postherpetic neuralgia: **gabapentin**/pregabalin, lidocaine patch; TCA anticholinergic in elderly; no late antiviral

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent pain >90 days, secondary bacterial infection, corneal injury, vision loss
Meningoencephalitis, vasculopathy, visceral spread in vulnerable patients

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Shingrix two doses** for adults ≥50 years or immunocompromised ≥19 years, including prior zoster
Cover lesions, **avoid susceptible contacts** until crusted; exposure causes chickenpox, not immediate shingles
Disseminated: airborne/contact until crusted; immunocompromised localized: same precautions until dissemination excluded

rows.label: Mimics
items: HSV: recurrent localized lesions, often oral/genital rather than a full dermatome
Contact dermatitis: prominent itch, exposure pattern, no neuropathic prodrome

huntington-disease.name: Huntington disease
huntington-disease.scope: CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion, anticipation, chorea, caudate and putamen atrophy, psychiatric manifestations
huntington-disease.core: An inherited progressive movement, cognitive, and psychiatric disorder often emerges in midlife, with earlier onset across successive generations.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Autosomal dominant HTT CAG expansion**; each child of an affected heterozygote has 50% risk
Paternal transmission particularly associated with repeat expansion and anticipation

rows.label: Clues
items: Irregular flowing chorea, motor impersistence, impaired voluntary saccades; later rigidity and bradykinesia
Irritability, depression, impulsivity, psychosis; executive dysfunction progresses to dementia
Psychiatric symptoms may precede movement disorder; juvenile disease often rigid with seizures
★ **Suicidal ideation** requires direct safety assessment, especially around diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Toxic huntingtin damages striatal GABAergic neurons; reduced indirect-pathway inhibition increases unwanted movement
Caudate/putamen atrophy produces enlarged frontal horns on brain imaging

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Compatible phenotype/family history → **HTT genetic testing** after informed counseling
≥40 repeats: full penetrance; 36–39: reduced penetrance; intermediate alleles can expand in offspring
MRI supports differential diagnosis; gene testing confirms, imaging alone does not
Predictive testing of asymptomatic adults → consent, psychological assessment and genetic counseling

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling chorea → **tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine**; monitor depression, suicidality and parkinsonism
Antipsychotics such as risperidone for psychosis/aggression; SSRIs for depression/anxiety
Physical/occupational and speech-swallow support; nutrition, fall prevention and advance-care planning
No established cure; avoid dopamine-depleting agents in active suicidality or inadequately treated depression

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, falls, weight loss, loss of independence; suicide
VMAT2 inhibitors → sedation, akathisia, depression; antipsychotics → metabolic and motor adverse effects

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reproductive counseling, prenatal/preimplantation testing options; defer predictive testing of asymptomatic minors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Wilson disease: younger onset, liver disease, low ceruloplasmin; potentially treatable
Tardive dyskinesia: dopamine-blocker exposure, predominant orobuccolingual stereotypies

huntington-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

hyponatremia.name: Hyponatremia
hyponatremia.scope: Hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH, primary polydipsia), hypervolemic, acute vs chronic, hypertonic saline indications
hyponatremia.core: Low serum sodium reflects excess water relative to sodium; symptoms and duration determine urgency before the cause determines maintenance treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, oxytocin; **hypotonic IV D5W**, postoperative state, exercise + excess water
Pulmonary/CNS disease; **small cell lung cancer** (ectopic ADH); heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, headache, gait instability; seizures, coma or marked confusion indicate severe cerebral edema
Orthostasis/dry mucosa suggest depletion; edema/ascites suggest excess extracellular fluid
SIADH: clinically euvolemic with inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolality
Massive water intake, often psychiatric illness; urine osmolality below serum still favors polydipsia, even if >100

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into brain; chronic adaptation makes rapid correction dangerous
ADH-mediated water retention or intake exceeding renal dilution capacity lowers sodium concentration
Low effective volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, diarrhea) → baroreceptor ADH release; total-body sodium high in edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serum osmolality first: **<275 mOsm/kg** confirms hypotonicity; assess glucose and volume status
Hyperglycemia → translocational hyponatremia; severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia → pseudohyponatremia
★ Urine osmolality **<100** → polydipsia/low solute; ≥100 → persistent ADH activity
Urine Na <20–30 suggests low effective arterial volume; >30 suggests renal loss or SIADH
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and renal failure before diagnosing SIADH; diuretics confound urine Na

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe neurologic symptoms → **3% saline bolus**, repeated for initial Na rise 4–6 mEq/L
Hypovolemia → isotonic saline; SIADH → fluid restriction, increased solute, remove trigger
Edematous states → fluid/sodium restriction and loop diuretic; treat heart/liver/kidney disorder
★ Chronic/unknown duration: generally limit rise to **≤8 mEq/L per 24 h**; monitor frequently
Overcorrection → desmopressin plus D5W; avoid routine vaptans in acute symptomatic cases

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute severe hyponatremia → herniation, respiratory arrest
Osmotic demyelination after rapid correction; greatest risk with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids during high ADH states; review causative drugs
Monitor for brisk aquaresis after restoring volume or stopping thiazides

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cerebral salt wasting: neurosurgical patient, hypovolemic, high urine Na; SIADH euvolemic
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemia: measured osmolality elevated
Primary psychiatric disease: neurologic change without sodium abnormality

hyponatremia.evidence: Not checked online; established hyponatremia consensus principles.

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage (most common) or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids/vitamin A supplements

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late, compensatory; treat ICP, not BP
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema
IIH: **impaired CSF resorption** at arachnoid granulations; ventricles normal/small, no obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings → **LP**: normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction
Recent shunt revision + fever + neutrophilic CSF → **shunt infection**, not community meningitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway/intubation first**, head elevation, IV **hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

infective-endocarditis.name: Infective endocarditis
infective-endocarditis.scope: Native and prosthetic valve endocarditis, Duke criteria, prophylaxis, IV drug use endocarditis, blood culture diagnostic criteria
infective-endocarditis.core: Persistent bacteremia with valve infection causes systemic emboli, valve destruction, and immune-complex injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prosthetic valve, prior endocarditis, congenital valve abnormality, intracardiac device
Injection drug use → tricuspid involvement; healthcare exposure, indwelling vascular access

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, new regurgitant murmur, embolic stroke, splenic infarct, hematuria
Janeway lesions painless; Osler nodes painful; Roth spots retinal; splinter hemorrhages nonspecific
★ **New conduction block** → periannular abscess; right-sided disease → septic pulmonary emboli

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Endothelial injury → platelet-fibrin nidus → microbial adherence and vegetation
Immune complexes → glomerulonephritis; infected fragments disseminate through downstream circulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Three blood-culture sets before antibiotics**; separate peripheral draws unless resuscitation would be delayed
Major microbiology: **typical organism in ≥2 culture sets**, nontypical in ≥3; specialized serology/PCR also qualifies
★ **TTE → TEE** if prosthesis/high suspicion; major imaging: vegetation, abscess, perforation, new significant regurgitation
Definite clinical Duke: 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria
Minor: predisposition, fever, vascular phenomena, immunologic phenomena, nondiagnostic microbiology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Empiric **IV vancomycin + cefepime** for acutely ill/healthcare-associated cases; tailor to cultures and setting
MSSA → nafcillin/oxacillin or cefazolin; susceptible viridans streptococci → ceftriaxone
Prolonged pathogen-directed IV antibiotics; prosthetic infections need specialist regimen and early surgical evaluation
Surgery: heart failure, abscess, persistent bacteremia, fungal infection, or selected recurrent/large embolizing vegetations

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute regurgitation, heart failure, mycotic aneurysm, metastatic infection
Antibiotic nephrotoxicity, line infection; hemorrhage into embolic cerebral lesions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Dental **amoxicillin** for prosthetic valve/material, previous IE, selected cyanotic/residual CHD, transplant valvulopathy
Good oral hygiene, sterile access; no routine prophylaxis for GI/GU procedures or isolated MVP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis: cancer/autoimmune disease, sterile cultures
Atrial myxoma: positional obstruction, intracavitary mass; vasculitis: no infected vegetation

inflammatory-myopathies.name: Inflammatory myopathies
inflammatory-myopathies.scope: Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, elevated creatine kinase, autoantibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2), muscle biopsy, malignancy screening, systemic corticosteroids
inflammatory-myopathies.core: Objective muscle weakness with elevated muscle enzymes suggests myopathy; distribution, skin findings, and biopsy distinguish treatable inflammation from inclusion body disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune predisposition; adult dermatomyositis associated with occult malignancy
Inclusion body myositis: usually men >50 years; review statin and other myotoxic exposures

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Difficulty rising or lifting arms**, neck flexor weakness; sensation and reflexes generally preserved
Dysphagia, aspiration, dyspnea warrant evaluation for bulbar/respiratory weakness and interstitial lung disease
Dermatomyositis can have characteristic rash before significant muscle weakness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Polymyositis: T-cell-mediated endomysial injury; dermatomyositis: complement-associated microvascular injury
Inclusion body disease combines inflammatory and degenerative pathology, explaining poor immunosuppressive response

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK, aldolase, AST/ALT**, TSH; muscle can explain transaminase elevation without primary liver disease
Proximal weakness + ↑CK → EMG/nerve conduction (myopathic pattern); MRI guides **muscle biopsy**
★ **Anti-Jo-1**: antisynthetase syndrome with ILD, arthritis, mechanic's hands; **anti-Mi-2**: classic dermatomyositis
Check swallowing and lung function when symptomatic; exclude inherited, endocrine, and drug-induced myopathies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Polymyositis/dermatomyositis → **systemic glucocorticoids + steroid-sparing agent**, such as methotrexate or azathioprine
Severe/refractory disease or dysphagia → IVIG or other specialist-directed immunomodulation
Inclusion body: PT/OT, mobility aids, swallowing support; immunosuppression usually ineffective
Dermatomyositis rash: sun protection and topical agents; rehabilitation without prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, respiratory failure, ILD, myocarditis; juvenile dermatomyositis can cause calcinosis
Steroid myopathy causes new weakness with normal CK; treatment also increases infection and fracture risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adult dermatomyositis → **age-based plus risk-based malignancy evaluation**, especially near diagnosis
Bone protection, immunizations, infection prophylaxis according to immunosuppressive intensity; monitor strength and CK

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polymyalgia rheumatica: pain/stiffness without true weakness or ↑CK
Myasthenia: fatigability, ocular symptoms, normal CK; ALS: mixed UMN/LMN signs
Guillain-Barré: ascending distal-predominant weakness, areflexia
